newsitem.title: USA: Banks elated, Wall Street deflated by Fed vote.
newsitem.headline: Banks elated, Wall Street deflated by Fed vote.

text.p: Federal Reserve's decision on Friday to allow banks to increase their underwriting activities left banks celebrating and securities firms growling.

The Fed voted to allow so-called section 20 subsidiaries of banks to derive as much as 25 percent of their revenue from underwriting and dealing in securities such as stocks and bonds, up from the current 10 percent limit.
"We're very pleased," Rachel Robbins, general counsel of J.P. Morgan & Co, said. "We think it's well within existing law."
J.P. Morgan projected it would bump up against the old 10 percent cap sooner or later, Robbins said. "Clearly what this does is allow us to continue to grow our business," she said.
Earlier this year, the Fed took enforcement action against Swiss Bank Corp for exceeding the cap.
Banks expect much of the newly permitted growth will come on underwriting deals for foreign companies.
"This allows banks to serve a wider global market," said Rich Whiting, general counsel of the bankers roundtable, a trade group representing over 100 large banks.
Banks can now "compete with those large overseas underwriters and doemstic underwriter who don't have any limitations in serveing overseas companies," Whiting said.
American Bankers Association also praised the ruling.
"We congratulate the Fed for leading the way in bringing the financial services industry into the 21st century," Larry LaRocco, managing director of the group, said.

Not all banks were supportive, however. Independent Bankers Association of America, a trade group representing 5,500 independent community banks, said the change would "restructure and further concentrate the financial services industry."
Such matters "had been best left for the Congress," the group said.
Securities firms said the Fed's action created an unfair playing field. Banks can compete in securities, but securities firms can do little in the field of banking, they said.

"Piecemeal decisions by the banking regulators are rapidly expanding the financial services that banks can provide while securities firms remain constrained by the Depression-era laws," Steve Judge, senior vice president of the Securities Industry Association, said.

At least in public, banks said they still support Congressional reform efforts. "We need complete financial reform," J.P. Morgan's Robbins said. "This addreses one piece of it and doesn't address it completely but until Congress can act this is a welcome action."

"We have long supported comprehensive reform and long opposed piecemeal reform," Merrill Lynch & Co director of government relations Bruce Thompson said. "Congress, not the regulators or the courts, should be the ones to act."
Thompson said he hoped the greater latitude given to banks would not reduce the banks previous support for Congressional action.
"We hope this does not reduce their incentive," he said. "The time really is coming for having everyone put aside their own particular interests and support comprehensive reform."
